questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Identify how question order changes ratings on a customer form
questions.stem: A bistro asks guests to rate its new tasting menu, and the first question mentions the chef's reputation before asking for ratings.

options.text: Order can shift ratings because earlier questions prime how guests interpret the later rating scale.
Guests who lead with the chef's name always score the tasting menu lower than those who do not.
options.misconception: Believes priming always pushes scores downward

options.text: Any shift in ratings across versions is caused by differences in the sample of guests who replied.
options.misconception: Assumes every shift comes from sampling error

options.text: Order effects disappear whenever the rating scale runs from one to five with printed labels.
options.misconception: Believes a labelled scale removes all order effects

questions.explanation: Earlier items can prime answers to later ones, so the same menu may score differently by order. A labelled scale does not remove priming, and sampling error cannot cause a consistent shift across randomised versions.
questions.hint: Think about what the earlier question primes.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Interpret what a small pretest can and cannot show
questions.stem: A café pretests two layouts of a printed menu, giving version A to 20 customers and version B to a different 20, and records which dish each names first.

options.text: Because the groups differed, the difference in named dishes cannot be attributed to layout alone.
The higher-priced version naming more first shows that price drives customers to notice it.
options.misconception: Treats a price effect as the only explanation

options.text: With 40 customers tested, the layout effect is established strongly enough to act on.
options.misconception: Believes the sample size alone proves the effect

options.text: Since both versions were shown in one week, the test provides a clean read on preference.
options.misconception: Assumes same-week testing removes every confound

questions.explanation: Pretesting is exploratory, and the two groups were not randomly assigned, so they may differ in ways beyond layout. The pattern suggests questions to follow up, not a settled conclusion.
questions.hint: Pretests screen ideas; they rarely settle them.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Explain how sampling and frame error affect an estimate
questions.stem: A restaurant asks 30 of its 900 covers a month how likely they are to return, and the owner wants to know the true rate for the whole restaurant.

answer.exemplar: The 30 covers form a convenience sample from one site, so the estimate carries sampling error from who happened to be surveyed and nonresponse from those who declined, plus coverage error because diners of other sites, delivery orders and bookings are missing. The figure should be presented as an estimate with a wide margin rather than the true rate.

questions.explanation: The gap between the estimate and the truth comes from sampling error, which widens with small samples, and frame error, since one site's diners exclude others. Nonresponse adds bias on top.
questions.hint: Name the error types, not just 'small sample'.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Compute coverage of a supplier frame
questions.stem: A bakery's supplier frame lists 120 suppliers; the chef buys from 96 of them in a year, so coverage of the buying frame is what percentage?
questions.explanation: Coverage here is the share of frame members represented, 96 of 120 suppliers, which equals 80 percent. The other 24 were never bought from, so their costs never enter the estimate.
questions.hint: Divide the represented members by all frame members.

questions.learningObjective: Order the steps for building a single-construct scale
questions.stem: A taste-test form measures several different things at once; put the steps in the order that produces a valid single-construct measure.

options.text: Define the construct, drop items on other constructs, pilot the reduced scale, check survivors share one meaning.
Pilot the full form, define the construct from what the items happen to cover, then drop items that do not fit.
options.misconception: Defines the construct from the items, reversing the logic

options.text: Define the construct, pilot the reduced scale, keep every original item, then drop the items on other constructs.
options.misconception: Keeps every item, so the scale stays multi-construct

options.text: Drop items on other constructs, define the construct later, pilot the reduced scale, then check the remaining items.
options.misconception: Removes items before knowing what the construct is

questions.explanation: A valid scale starts from a construct definition, drops items on other constructs, and pilots the survivors to check they share one meaning. Defining the construct after pilotising reverses that logic.
questions.hint: Definition first, pruning second, pilot last.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Choose a change that makes portion definitions comparable

stimulus.body: Line 41 reads: one portion equals one filled ladle of braise to the level of the brass band. Line 58 reads: one portion equals 240 grams. Line 63 reads: one portion equals one dinner plate, filled. All three lines are priced at the same unit cost in the weekly costing sheet.

questions.stem: Using the costing sheet excerpt above, which single change would make the three portion definitions comparable across recipes?

options.text: Convert each definition to grams using measured yields, so every line reports portions in the same unit.
Price all three lines at the same rate per portion and call the definitions aligned with each other.
options.misconception: Believes a shared price hides different physical quantities

options.text: Keep the ladle and plate measures but ask each cook to report portions to the nearest quarter.
options.misconception: Confuses rounding precision with a common measurement unit

options.text: Replace the gram measure with the ladle measure on the lines that currently use grams.
options.misconception: Changes one unit to another unit without any conversion

questions.explanation: Operational definitions align when expressed in the same unit, so converting each to grams with tested yields aligns them. A shared price hides quantity differences; swapping units without conversion aligns nothing.

questions.learningObjective: Separate confound identification from remedy in a comparison
questions.stem: A kitchen compares braised short rib at 63 degrees with 68 degrees; the 68 degree batch is also the one tasted later in the evening and by a hungrier panel. Which step comes first?

options.text: Name late tasting and hunger as confounds of temperature, then repeat with balanced order and matched appetite.
Measure core temperature first, then repeat the taste test after the panel has eaten a full meal.
options.misconception: Treats a full meal as a fix for carryover from earlier tastings

options.text: Taste both batches in the same session, then pool scores across chefs to stabilise the estimate.
options.misconception: Assumes more raters removes the confound of order and hunger

options.text: Run the higher temperature in the morning, then report whichever batch scores better overall.
options.misconception: Keeps the order confound while choosing the winner by score

questions.explanation: Late tasting and hunger vary with the temperature, so the difference cannot be attributed to temperature alone. Naming those confounds, then balancing order and matching appetite, separates the factors.

options.text: The measure lacks content validity because it samples one narrow slice of the experience it claims to cover.
The measure has content validity because it asks directly about the thing customers care about most.
options.misconception: Equates a direct question with full content coverage

options.misconception: Believes content validity depends on later recipe changes

options.text: The measure has content validity as long as the sample size reaches a few hundred respondents.
options.misconception: Confuses sample size with the breadth of the measure

questions.explanation: Content validity asks whether items sample the whole domain the conclusion claims to cover. Tastiness alone misses service, price and atmosphere, and a large sample adds no breadth.

questions.learningObjective: Read a randomised order comparison for an order effect
questions.stem: Half of 400 dine-in guests see the satisfaction question after a complaint question and half before it; the complaint-first group rates 6.8 and the other 7.4.

options.text: The order of the two questions is a plausible cause of the 0.6 point gap, so ratings are not order-independent.
The 0.6 point gap is too small to matter, so the order effect should be ignored in reporting.
options.misconception: Treats a half-point rating gap as automatically unimportant

options.text: Guests who complain more harshly also rate the kitchen lower, which fully explains the difference.
options.misconception: Attributes the whole gap to complaining style rather than order

options.text: Since both groups had 400 guests, random assignment of order was unnecessary for a fair comparison.
options.misconception: Believes equal group sizes substitute for random assignment

questions.explanation: A stable 0.6 gap across 200 randomised guests per group points to an order effect, not noise. Randomisation balances complaint-prone guests; equal group sizes alone do not remove order effects.
questions.hint: Order was randomised, so what differs?

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Explain the limits of a three-person pretest
questions.stem: A pizzeria pretests a new crust name with three customers before printing menus, and the owner plans to use the reaction as proof the name will sell.

answer.exemplar: A pretest with three people is a usability check, not market evidence. Their reactions show whether the name is confusing or unappealing to a few listeners, which is useful for catching bad wording, but it cannot establish demand or forecast sales because the sample is tiny, unrepresentative and unreplicated.

questions.explanation: Pretesting screens for confusion before launch: three reactions can rule out a bad name but cannot support a sales claim. Generalising needs a proper sample and real buying data.
questions.hint: Pretests catch problems; they do not forecast sales.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the standard error of a sample mean
questions.stem: A caterer wants the average cost of 60 plated meals; she costs 25 of them, and the 25 costed meals average 6.40 each with a standard deviation of 1.20. What is the standard error of the mean?
questions.explanation: Standard error of the mean divides the standard deviation by the square root of the case count: 1.20 over the root of 25 gives 0.24. The standard deviation alone describes single meals.
questions.hint: Divide the deviation by the root of the sample size.

questions.learningObjective: Order the steps that produce good frame coverage
questions.stem: A market researcher surveys diners to estimate the city's restaurant spending; put the steps in the order that produces good frame coverage.

options.text: Define the target population, list every eligible diner, then sample from that list and check the achieved sample against it.
Sample diners in the busiest quarter, then check how many agreed to answer, then adjust the figures for refusals.
options.misconception: Treats the busiest quarter as the frame and refusals as error

options.text: Ask each respondent to name other diners, then survey that list, then average the results across all interviews.
options.misconception: Uses respondent referral as if it were a complete frame

options.text: Survey one street of restaurants, then multiply the average ticket by the number of restaurants in the city.
options.misconception: Scales one street up without checking coverage

questions.explanation: Good coverage needs the target population named, every eligible member listed, and the achieved sample checked against it. Busy quarters, referrals and single streets substitute convenience for a frame.
questions.hint: Frame first, sample second, check coverage third.

questions.learningObjective: Group items into a single-construct measure of flavour

stimulus.body: Tasting card, line 1: How was the tenderness of the beef? Line 2: How was the service? Line 3: How was the price for your meal? Line 4: Would you recommend us? Line 5: How was the flavour of the sauce? All five lines use the same five-point scale.

questions.stem: Given the score card above, which revision best turns it into a single-construct measure of sauce flavour?

options.text: Keep the flavour and tenderness items together and report them separately from service, price, and recommendation.
Average all five lines into one satisfaction score so the card measures overall satisfaction.
options.misconception: Averages unrelated attributes into one satisfaction score

options.text: Keep only the recommendation line, since it best captures what customers thought of the sauce.
options.misconception: Treats recommendation as a proxy for sauce flavour

options.text: Ask one combined question that mentions tenderness, service, price, sauce, and recommendation together.
options.misconception: Bundles every attribute into a single overlapping question

questions.explanation: A single-construct measure taps one attribute and separates the rest. Averaging unrelated lines creates a satisfaction construct instead, and recommendation is a different judgement, not a flavour item.
questions.hint: Group by attribute, then report each separately.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Convert two portion definitions into one comparable unit
questions.stem: Two kitchens record the same soup; the first writes 300 millilitres per bowl and the second writes 3 ladles per bowl with a ladle holding 100 millilitres. Which step comes first?

options.text: Convert the ladle count to millilitres using the known ladle volume, then compare the two bowls on one unit.
Compare the two bowls as written, because 3 ladles reads as a smaller number than 300 millilitres.
options.misconception: Compares unlike units because the numbers look different

options.text: Ask each kitchen to re-measure its bowls, then keep whichever figure the head chefs prefer.
options.misconception: Lets preference decide what an operational definition should be

options.text: Average 300 millilitres and 3 ladles to get a middle figure for both kitchens.
options.misconception: Averages incompatible units to manufacture a shared value

questions.explanation: Operational definitions align by converting to one unit: 3 ladles of 100 millilitres equals 300 millilitres. Comparing unlike units or averaging them leaves the two records unaligned.
questions.hint: Convert one unit using a known relation.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Identify confounds that vary with the comparison factor
questions.stem: A bistro compares two wine pairings, but the tasting for the pricier pairing happens in a quieter room with a different server.

options.text: Room noise and server behaviour vary with the pairing, so the comparison confounds price with those features.
The comparison is clean because only the wine changes and every other variable is irrelevant.
options.misconception: Assumes every other variable is irrelevant to judgement

options.text: The comparison is invalid only if the two wines cost more than five pounds apart.
options.misconception: Sets a price threshold for when a comparison becomes valid

options.text: The comparison is acceptable because both pairings were tasted in the same building.
options.misconception: Treats shared buildings as making the two settings identical

questions.explanation: A confound varies with the factor tested and could explain the result. Noise and service differ with the pairing, so price cannot be credited; one building does not equalise room or server.
questions.hint: Ask what else changed at the same time.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Match a conclusion to the coverage of the instrument
questions.stem: A cafe survey asks about taste, service, and value but the manager concludes only that guests found the coffee good.

options.text: The conclusion is narrower than the instrument, so it avoids the breadth the survey could have supported.
The conclusion is invalid because the survey measured three things instead of exactly one thing.
options.misconception: Treats multiple items as automatically destroying validity

options.text: The conclusion is invalid because taste cannot be measured by questionnaire at all.
options.misconception: Claims taste is beyond the reach of self-report data

options.text: The conclusion is sound because the survey included the item about coffee quality itself.
options.misconception: Believes one included item covers every domain claimed

questions.explanation: Content validity concerns the match between items covered and the claim made. Narrowing the claim to coffee quality keeps it inside the instrument's coverage, so several items with a modest claim are consistent.
questions.hint: Compare the claim with what the items cover.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Explain how placement of a global rating shapes answers
questions.stem: A catering client is asked the overall satisfaction question before and after a question about food presentation on the same form.

answer.exemplar: Placing the overall satisfaction question first gives respondents no earlier material to build on, so they answer from their own overall impression and from the meal just eaten. Put after the presentation question, they may anchor their general verdict on a single visual detail, which is a narrower basis than the word overall implies.

questions.explanation: Order decides what information respondents have when answering the overall item, so a preceding narrow question can anchor a global judgement. Asking the global question first captures the undirected impression.
questions.hint: Think about what comes before the global rating.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Compute the share of tasters who understood a description
questions.stem: A chef pretests a menu item with 25 tasters and 9 report the wording was confusing; the chef wants the percentage of tasters who understood the item description.
questions.explanation: Nine of twenty-five were confused, so 16 understood and 16 over 25 equals 64 percent. The share who understood is therefore 100 minus 64, which is 36 percent, not the confusion rate itself.
questions.hint: Compute the complement of the confusion rate.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Order the steps for an unbiased estimate of ticket value
questions.stem: A sandwich shop wants an unbiased estimate of average ticket value; arrange the steps that keep sampling error small and unbiased.

options.text: Define the target of all transactions, draw a random sample across days and hours, then weight and report with an uncertainty range.
Ask staff which sandwiches sell best, use those to pick a sample, then report the average ticket with no range.
options.misconception: Uses staff picks as a proxy for a random sample

options.text: Survey the busiest hour of a weekday only, because the busiest hour is the most representative of the shop.
options.misconception: Equates busiest hours with representative sampling

options.text: Collect every ticket from one slow Tuesday, treat it as the population, and describe it as the sampling frame.
options.misconception: Calls one day's tickets a frame and a population

questions.explanation: Unbiased estimates come from defining the population, drawing a random sample across varied times, and reporting an uncertainty range. Staff picks and single days trade randomness for convenience.
questions.hint: Random across varied times, then report the range.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Diagnose coverage error in a sampling note

stimulus.body: The sampling note for a supermarket survey reads: frame = all loyalty members with at least one purchase in the last twelve months. Achieved sample = 480 members drawn from that frame. Weekly note from the analyst: 62 members in the frame bought nothing this month; 44 members aged under 30 did not respond to the first call.

questions.stem: Using the sampling note above, which statement best describes the coverage problem in this survey?

options.text: The frame itself omits recent first-time buyers, so even a full sample of it would under-cover the shopping population.
Coverage is complete because 480 members were drawn from a frame that already matched the study's definition.
options.misconception: Assumes drawing from a frame proves the frame was complete

options.text: The only problem is nonresponse from 44 members, since the frame was built correctly from purchase records.
options.misconception: Reduces the whole coverage question to nonresponse alone

options.text: Coverage is perfect for all customers except those who bought nothing this month, who are irrelevant to the study.
options.misconception: Treats inactive shoppers as irrelevant rather than uncounted

questions.explanation: Coverage asks whether every population member could enter the frame. First-time buyers never appear in twelve-month records, so the frame misses them however well the chosen members respond.
questions.hint: Ask who could never enter the frame at all.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Sequence construct definition before scale combination
questions.stem: A hotel survey includes items on bed comfort, noise, breakfast and staff; the analyst wants one satisfaction score. Which step comes first?

options.text: Decide whether satisfaction is the construct of interest, then check that the items chosen to represent it all tap it.
Average the four items into one score, then describe the result as a single satisfaction measure without further checks.
options.misconception: Averages unrelated attributes and treats the result as valid

options.text: Ask the analyst which of the four items they prefer, then build the scale around that one item alone.
options.misconception: Chooses an item by preference rather than by construct fit

options.text: Report each of the four item scores separately and call the set one satisfaction score.
options.misconception: Calls a set of separate scores one single score

questions.explanation: Deciding the construct first prevents averaging attributes that do not belong to it. Only when the chosen items all tap that construct can their combination be read as one satisfaction score.
questions.hint: Name the construct before you combine items.

options.misconception: Picks the larger figure to keep records internally consistent

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a single item fails a broader validity claim
questions.stem: A grocer plans to claim that shoppers find the store easy to navigate, using a single question about how clearly signs are written.

answer.exemplar: The instrument measures the legibility of written signs, which is only one facet of whether a store can be navigated. questions.explanation: Content validity requires the items to sample the domain named in the conclusion. Sign legibility alone does not cover layout, placement, staff help, or shopper familiarity, so the navigation claim outruns the measure.

questions.hint: Subtract the smaller share from the larger.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Diagnose the main sampling error in a door intercept

stimulus.body: Survey log for a cafe satisfaction study. Goal: estimate satisfaction among all cafe customers on a weekday morning. Sampling method: intercept at the door, every fourth customer leaving between 8 and 10 am. Refusals: 31 of 240 intercepts. Follow-up: 9 of the 209 respondents called back had visited another branch the same morning.

questions.stem: Using the survey log above, which source of sampling error is the door intercept most clearly introducing?

options.text: Coverage error, because weekday morning regulars at other sites are missing from the frame the intercept creates.
Sampling error only, because intercepting every fourth customer is a random sample of the morning crowd.
options.misconception: Calls systematic interception a random sample

options.text: Nonresponse bias only, because the 31 refusals are the sole source of bias in the estimate.
options.misconception: Points at refusals while ignoring who was never intercepted

options.text: Measurement error only, because some respondents visited another branch during the same morning.
options.misconception: Labels a frame problem as a measurement problem

questions.explanation: The intercept creates a frame of one site, one morning, one hour, so other branches and times are absent, which is coverage error. Randomising within it cannot repair that.
questions.hint: Ask who was never even in the running.

options.text: Ask the billing office which non-billed patients matter most and sample only those groups.
options.misconception: Uses staff judgement to pick a partial frame on purpose

questions.explanation: Coverage must be checked before sampling, because a frame that omits a category cannot be repaired by more draws from it. Comparing the billed list with all service users identifies the gap.
questions.hint: Frame gaps cannot be fixed by more sampling.

questions.learningObjective: Identify a form that mixes several constructs
questions.stem: A cafe loyalty form asks how often the guest visits, how much they spend, and how happy they are with the coffee, all on one overall score.

options.misconception: Adds a cue that strengthens rather than weakens the anchor

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Compute the misreading rate in a pretest
questions.stem: A packaging pretest shows 8 of 12 shoppers read a label as 'per serving' when it meant 'per pack', after five shoppers had already commented on the number.

options.text: Two thirds misread the label, which is a serious wording problem worth fixing before any wider use.
One third misread the label, so the wording is mostly working and can go out as it is.
options.misconception: Reports the complement of the misreading rate

options.text: The misreading rate shows the panel is unreliable, since eight shoppers cannot read a simple label.
options.misconception: Blames the respondents rather than the wording

options.text: The misreading rate is a sampling artifact, since only twelve shoppers saw the design at all.
options.misconception: Treats a wording failure as a sampling artifact

questions.explanation: Eight of twelve is two thirds misreading, a substantive defect in the label rather than a rounding concern. Small samples make the estimate imprecise but do not explain a wording failure.
questions.hint: Convert misreadings to a proportion first.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Describe the period a wait time estimate actually covers
questions.stem: A clinic wants the average wait time reported for all its patients, but it can only time visits from the week it installed a new screen.

answer.exemplar: The patients seen in that week define the sample, and if weekday mornings and busy clinic sessions are over-represented among them, their wait times will differ systematically from the full patient list. The estimate should be reported as the average for that week with its uncertainty, and any claim about all patients should note that patients outside the observation window were never measured at all.

questions.explanation: Wait times vary by day and hour, so a single-week sample can be biased relative to the full patient list. Report the week's average with an uncertainty range and keep any general claim within it.
questions.hint: Say which period the average actually describes.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Compute the composition of a survey frame
questions.stem: A frame for a catering survey lists 900 named contacts, of which 45 percent are catering firms and the rest are private hires; how many private-hire contacts are in the frame?
questions.explanation: Private hires are 100 minus 45, which is 55 percent of the frame, and 55 percent of 900 is 495 contacts. Reading the 45 percent as private hires would actually count the firms.
questions.hint: Take the complement, then multiply by the frame.
